title: Data Provenance Auditing of Fine-Tuned Large Language Models with a Text-Preserving Technique
claim: A marking-and-querying procedure embeds hidden cue/reply watermarks in data, then detects their use in a model with a bounded false-positive rate.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right, numbered steps 1-5 above a phase timeline
description: A single wide diagram reads left to right along a bottom timeline split into three phases: generation and attribution, watermark embedding, and watermark detection and decision. On the left, a sensitive collection of document icons D1…Di feeds into a set of watermarks W (the target watermark w plus counterfactuals). In the middle, a document stack is marked with green cue-syllable dots and blue reply-syllable dots, producing the published marked collection. On the right, cue chunks are fed into a boxed 'suspicious model' L, and a magnifying glass searches the output for reply syllables. Black numbered circles 1–5 mark the steps. Red arrows and text at the top pose the question 'Is D^w partly included in D'?' and the answer 'Yes/No, with a reliable FPR bound'. Green and blue colour-code cue and reply, and the eye goes first to the red question at the top.
caption: Overview of the proposal. A user is attributed a set WK of K watermarks and commits to one, w, which is embedded into their sensitive collection prior to release. At audit time, the model is queried using the cue of each watermark of WK, which may elicit the corresponding reply. The target watermark w is then ranked against counterfactuals. If it exceeds a fixed threshold k, we infer that sensitive data was included in the model’s fine-tuning set.
abstract: We propose a system for marking sensitive or copyrighted texts to detect their use in fine-tuning large language models under black-box access with statistical guarantees. Our method builds digital ``marks'' using invisible Unicode characters organized into (``cue'', ``reply'') pairs. During an audit, prompts containing only ``cue'' fragments are issued to trigger regurgitation of the corresponding ``reply'', indicating document usage. To control false positives, we compare against held-out counterfactual marks and apply a ranking test, yielding a verifiable bound on the false positive rate. Empirically, we obtain a true positive rate of 96.7% at 0% false positive rate and reply regurgitation rates exceeding 28% per document with only 40 (4%) watermarked documents. The approach is minimally invasive, scalable across many sources, robust to standard processing pipelines, and achieves high detection power even when marked data is a small fraction of the fine-tuning corpus.
